vignette:
She is 32 and works as a city council member, a role she once experienced as a point of pride and purpose. Before the disaster, her days are full but manageable: long meetings, community events, late-night calls from constituents, and the familiar rhythm of public service. She describes herself as someone who likes being useful, someone who can keep moving even when tired. That steadiness changes after the man-made disaster, which she experiences not as a distant headline but as a sudden collapse of the world she had been helping to hold together.

The event unfolds in a public space she knows well, during a community gathering tied to her council work. There is chaos, smoke, shouting, and a confusion she cannot fully make sense of in the moment. She remembers fragments more clearly than the whole: the sound first, then the heat, then seeing people run in directions that do not help. As others scream for help, she freezes briefly, then moves on instinct, trying to guide people to safety and get information to emergency responders. In the days afterward, she tells herself that because she was functional, because she kept others moving, she must be handling it. But the body seems to know something different. She startsle easily, feels a constant tightness in her chest, and notices that sleep no longer arrives naturally. When she closes her eyes, she sees flashes of the scene as if her mind is replaying the disaster without asking.

She returns to work quickly, partly from obligation and partly because being at home leaves too much room for memory. In council chambers she sits upright, attentive, measured, but her attention is fractured. Sudden noises from construction outside or a chair scraping the floor can make her jolt so sharply that she feels embarrassed by her own body. She begins scanning entrances, exits, and faces in every room she enters. She chooses seats with her back to the wall and watches windows more than speakers. Her colleagues notice that she seems more serious, more distant, and less willing to linger after meetings. She gives concise answers and keeps her voice controlled, yet inside she feels as though she is always bracing for another blow.

At night, she avoids sleep when she can. If she does sleep, she wakes with her heart pounding, drenched in sweat, unable to immediately place herself in the present. She has one recurring dream in which she is back at the gathering and cannot get people out in time. In the dream, she calls out but no sound comes. She wakes angry with herself, ashamed of the helplessness that returns with such force. During the day, she avoids the neighborhood where the disaster occurred and declines invitations to public events that might resemble that setting. She tells people she is busy. In reality, she is trying to outrun the surge of panic that rises when she imagines crowds, alarms, or the smell of smoke. Even ordinary sounds at home-the kettle whistling, a phone vibrating on the counter, a siren in the distance-can make her body tense before her mind catches up.

As a South Asian woman in public office, she feels an added pressure to be composed, resilient, and respectable. She has spent much of her life learning how to absorb distress without displaying it too openly. After the disaster, that habit becomes both armor and burden. She does not want to be seen as fragile, and she especially does not want her community to feel less secure because she appears shaken. So she keeps showing up, keeps speaking at meetings, keeps taking calls, but her energy is depleted by the effort of holding herself together. She feels detached from friends and family, as if she is observing their lives from a slight distance. Moments that used to matter-shared meals, laughter, small plans for the weekend-now feel muted, almost unreal.

Over time, she becomes more irritable and less patient with interruptions. She catches herself snapping at staff over minor delays, then feels guilty and ashamed afterward. Her concentration slips in ways that are hard to hide in her work: she rereads reports, loses track of conversations, and struggles to remember details she would previously have retained easily. She worries that people will see the change and interpret it as weakness or incompetence. At the same time, she is angry that the disaster has taken not only safety, but also the ease with which she once moved through the world.

Still, she keeps going. She continues to attend council sessions, answer constituents, and speak carefully in public. But she does so with a kind of vigilance that never fully turns off, as though part of her remains at the edge of that day, listening for what might happen next.
